land.text: Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu south of northern Tohoku, the part of the Jomon country that the jomon-period dossier hands to the Yayoi at 300 BCE

predecessors.note: The jomon-period dossier dissolves at -300 with this land as its successor 'yayoi-period'; Hokkaido and northern Tohoku went to the Epi-Jomon (no dossier).

land.text: the Nara Basin, where the Yamato Kingship 'is usually believed to have begun c. 250' (Kofun period page)

successors.note: The yamato dossier starts at 250 in Nara; the Yayoi page gives the end as AD 300 and the transition 'around the mid-3rd century', so the two overlap 250-300 in Nara. The rest of the Yayoi land has no dossier after 300 (the Kofun period is a period, not a state; Yamato's vassals begin at 350).

correction.text: Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu south of northern Tohoku: the Japanese archipelago without Okinawa and the Ryukyus (where the Jomon were mostly absent) and without Hokkaido, Aomori, Iwate and Akita (the Epi-Jomon country, per the jomon-period dossier). The Yayoi page: 'The earliest archaeological evidence of the Yayoi Period is found on northern Kyushu'; 'Yayoi culture quickly spread to the main island of Honshu'.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe; Cliopatria has no Yayoi row. The page gives no area and no map of extent: its only land statements are the northern Kyushu origin, the quick spread to Honshu, 'Kansai and Shikoku exhibited more pronounced Yayoi characteristics' and 'Kyushu, Okinawa, and the Tohoku region retained stronger Jomon traits'. The shape is the researcher's reading, inherited from the jomon-period dossier's handover (about 285,500 km2 by the gazetteer, 1,129 cells); the southern Tohoku prefectures (Miyagi, Yamagata, Fukushima) are inside it though the page does not name them. One shape for 600 years because the page dates no change of extent. Overlaps the yamato dossier's Nara keyframe in 250-300.

region.text: Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu south of northern Tohoku, the Jomon land taken by the Yayoi culture

ledger.note: 300 BCE: the Yayoi culture replaces the Jomon in Kyushu, Shikoku and southern Honshu. 'The Yayoi period is, generally, accepted to date from circa 300 BC to AD 300'; 'The earliest archaeological evidence of the Yayoi Period is found on northern Kyushu'; 'Yayoi culture quickly spread to the main island of Honshu, mixing with native Jomon culture'. The page gives no date for the spread, so the whole region is drawn from the start, as the jomon-period dossier hands it over; the History of Japan page adds 'the Yayoi radiated out from northern Kyushu, gradually supplanting the Jomon' and dates the onset 'around 400 BC' or, by radiocarbon, 1,000-800 BC. The page calls the earlier dates 'highly controversial'.

region.text: the Yayoi land outside the Nara Basin when the Kofun period begins

ledger.note: AD 300: the Yayoi period ends and the Kofun period begins ('an era in the history of Japan from about 300 to 538 AD'). Neither the Yayoi nor the Kofun page names a state holding the land outside the Yamato core in 300, so it is recorded as nobody's; the political entity known as Wa-koku had formed 'by the end of the 2nd century' (Yayoi page) but no extent is given. Page silent on any successor state here.

region.text: the Nara Basin, core of the Yamato Kingship

ledger.note: AD 300: the Yayoi period gives way to the Kofun period under the Yamato Kingship. 'It is generally considered that the Yayoi period transitioned into the Kofun period around the mid-3rd century' (Yayoi page); 'The Yamato Kingship is usually believed to have begun c. 250' and 'the oldest Japanese kofun is reportedly Hokenoyama Kofun in Sakurai, Nara, which dates to the late 3rd century' (Kofun page). The yamato dossier already holds Nara from 250.

certainty.note: No treaty, survey or administrative record fixes any Yayoi frontier; the extent is the researcher's reading of a prehistoric culture's range, and the northern edge (Epi-Jomon) is approximate.

sources.title: Yayoi period
sources.note: Identity, dates c. 300 BC - AD 300, northern Kyushu origin, spread to Honshu, transition to the Kofun around the mid-3rd century, Wa-koku by the end of the 2nd century; no infobox, no area.

sources.title: Kofun period
sources.note: Kofun dates (about 300 to 538; infobox c. 3rd century), Yamato Kingship begun c. 250, Hokenoyama Kofun in Nara; used for the 300 hand-over.

sources.title: History of Japan
sources.note: Second page for the Yayoi onset (around 400 BC; radiocarbon 1000-800 BC), 'radiated out from northern Kyushu', Book of Han (111 AD) and Wei account (240 AD); no standalone Yayoi section.

notes:
Yayoi period (c. 300 BC - AD 300) is a prehistoric culture and period, typed culture like its predecessor jomon-period, not a state; no area, extent map or regional dating on any of the three pages opened. Region = the jomon-period dossier's handover (Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu south of northern Tohoku), confidence 2.

To settle: (1) Epi-Jomon (Zoku-Jomon) for Hokkaido, Aomori, Iwate and Akita has no dossier; the jomon-period dossier records the loss to slug 'epi-jomon' at -300 (its page, Jomon period, was not opened by this batch). (2) The yamato dossier starts 250 on Nara while this one ends 300: the 250-300 overlap in the Nara Basin should go to the smaller-wins rule. The yamato found event has counterpart 'nobody', so no matching loss is written here. (3) After 300 the Yayoi land outside Nara has no dossier until yamato's vassal_start events at 350; 300-350 is nobody's land on the map unless a Kofun-culture or Wa dossier is added. (4) Dates: Yayoi page lead says c. 300 BC - AD 300, body says 'to the mid-3rd century AD', History of Japan says onset around 400 BC or, by radiocarbon, 1,000-800 BC ('highly controversial' on the Yayoi page). The dossier follows the lead. (5) Chinese records are not territory events: the Yayoi page has Wo mentioned in AD 57 and the Na state of Wo receiving a gold seal from Emperor Guangwu (Book of the Later Han), Wo in 257 in the Wei zhi, and Himiko ruling Wa after a 'major civil war'; no year is given for the civil war, so no war is listed. Han suzerainty over Na (northern Kyushu) belongs in the han-dynasty dossier if anyone wants it. (6) Okinawa/Ryukyu: the page says only that Okinawa 'retained stronger Jomon traits'; excluded as in the jomon-period dossier. No gazetteer names needed (Ryukyu, Hokkaido, Nara resolve).
